title: Sign here, he said yes
objective: Know the nurse's part in informed consent: confirm the signer is of legal age, competent and acting voluntarily, and escalate when the client does not understand the procedure, its risks or alternatives
secondaryObjectives: Know that a nurse who knows consent was not properly obtained and does not tell the provider or a supervisor can be held liable, and that treating without consent may be battery

brief.situation: 07:15 in a pre-operative holding area. You are Mr. Patel's nurse. He is 68 and scheduled for a laparoscopic gallbladder removal at 07:45. The surgical resident hands you the consent form on the way to the OR: 'He's agreed, just get it signed. I'll be in theater.'
handover: He received the ordered IV hydromorphone for pain at 06:55. He is drowsy.
His daughter is with him and offers to sign 'to save time'. He has no activated health care power of attorney; he makes his own decisions.

Unit policy: the surgeon obtains consent; the nurse witnesses only a signature given by an alert, informed client; a client who has had a sedating drug signs only when the surgeon judges him able; the OR charge nurse is told of any consent problem.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide whether this consent can be valid, what you may and may not do, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Sedation wears off over about half an hour. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The surgeon told within 5 minutes of finding the problem (unit policy).
The surgeon returns once he is alert, explains, and he decides: about 30 min.
Transport to the OR: about 5 min.

why.question: Can you witness this consent? What is your part, and what do you do?

parts.label: Can it be valid
parts.criteria: Not now: the client must be of legal age, competent, informed (procedure, risks, alternatives) and acting voluntarily; he is drowsy after an opioid, cannot teach back and is being pressured; his daughter is not his decision-maker.
parts.modelAnswer: No. He's 68 and makes his own decisions, but right now he's drowsy from hydromorphone, he can't tell me what the operation is, its risks or alternatives, and he's going along with his family. That isn't informed, voluntary consent, and his daughter can't sign for him.

parts.label: My part
parts.criteria: The surgeon obtains consent; the nurse witnesses only a valid signature, does not explain the procedure, escalates to the surgeon and the OR, advocates and documents; proceeding without valid consent may be battery and the nurse who knows and says nothing can be liable.
parts.modelAnswer: Getting consent is the surgeon's job; I only witness a valid signature. I call the surgeon to come back and explain when he's alert, tell the OR charge nurse to hold the case, support him to ask his questions, and document. If I let it go ahead, operating without consent may be battery, and I'd share the liability.

noProgress.rationale: A client left an hour with no one told that his consent is not valid is harm here.

invalidOp.headline: No valid consent
invalidOp.body: Consent belongs to an alert, informed client acting freely, obtained by the surgeon. A drowsy client's signature, or a relative's, is not valid; the nurse escalates instead of witnessing.

consented.headline: Consent protected
consented.body: You checked his understanding, saw it could not be valid, called the surgeon and the OR, and supported him to decide for himself. That is the expert path.

consentedGaps.headline: Consent obtained, with gaps
consentedGaps.body: Check how soon you called the surgeon, whether the OR was told and whether he and his daughter were supported.

time_up.headline: Unresolved
time_up.body: A consent problem goes to the surgeon and the OR within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Valid consent needs a client of legal age who is competent, informed of the procedure, its risks and alternatives, and choosing freely. Mr. Patel is 68 and his own decision-maker, but he is drowsy 20 minutes after hydromorphone, cannot teach back the operation, a risk or an alternative, and is going along with family pressure; his daughter has no authority to sign. The surgeon obtains consent; the nurse only witnesses a valid signature and does not explain the procedure. Call the surgeon to return when he is alert, tell the OR charge nurse to hold the start, support him to ask his questions, and document. Going ahead without valid consent may be battery, and a nurse who knows and says nothing can be held liable.

roleQ.ask: While you check: what does the nurse's witness signature on a consent form affirm?

choices.label: That this person signed the form
That the nurse explained the risks
That the nurse formally assessed capacity

roleQ.explain: The nurse often signs as a witness to the client's signature, affirming that person signed; providing the information is not the nurse's role.
